name: Aldol Condensation
summary: Two molecules of an aldehyde or ketone having α-H combine in dilute base to give a β-hydroxy carbonyl, which dehydrates on heating to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl.
mechanism: Base removes an α-H to give an enolate. The enolate carbon attacks the carbonyl carbon of a second molecule (C–C bond formation) to give an alkoxide, which is protonated to the β-hydroxy compound. Heating removes water by E1cB to give the conjugated enone.
keyPoints: At least one α-H is needed on the nucleophile partner
Aldehydes give aldols easily; ketones need Ba(OH)2 / Soxhlet setup as equilibrium is unfavourable
Dehydration is favoured by conjugation and heat
Carbon skeleton doubles in chain length (propanal gives 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal)
whenUsed: Building longer carbon chains in the lab and industry (e.g. 2-ethylhexanol from butanal).
applications: Test-type conversions of acetaldehyde to but-2-enal
jeeTips: HCHO and benzaldehyde have no α-H and do not self-aldol (they undergo Cannizzaro). Name the product from the IUPAC chain: aldol of CH3CHO is 3-hydroxybutanal. Counting carbons: n molecules of RCH2CHO give a 2n-carbon product. Ketone aldol product from acetone is 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one.

name: Crossed Aldol Condensation
productName: Mixture of four aldols (useful only when one partner lacks α-H)
summary: Aldol condensation between two different carbonyl compounds, both having α-H, gives a mixture of four products; it is synthetically useful only if one partner has no α-H.
mechanism: Each carbonyl can form an enolate and each can act as the electrophile, so two self-aldols and two cross-aldols form. If one partner (e.g. HCHO, ArCHO, (CH3)3CCHO) has no α-H it can only be the electrophile, giving a single cross product.
keyPoints: Both partners with α-H: 4 products
One partner without α-H (and a more reactive C=O): essentially one product
Aldehyde is a better electrophile than ketone
Dehydration gives conjugated enone
whenUsed: Targeted C–C bond formation using a non-enolisable aldehyde as electrophile.
applications: Formaldehyde + acetaldehyde route to pentaerythritol precursors

examples.eq: CH3CHO + CH3CH2CHO ->[dil. NaOH] four aldol products

examples.note: Tris(hydroxymethyl)acetaldehyde, then crossed Cannizzaro gives pentaerythritol

jeeTips: Count products: two enolisable carbonyls = 4 products (2 self + 2 cross). With stereo, aldol products also have chiral centres. If a question says one product only, look for HCHO/ArCHO/(CH3)3CCHO as a partner.

name: Claisen–Schmidt Condensation
summary: Crossed aldol condensation of an aromatic aldehyde (no α-H) with an aliphatic aldehyde or ketone (having α-H) in base to give an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl.
mechanism: Base converts the aliphatic ketone/aldehyde into its enolate, which attacks the non-enolisable ArCHO. The β-hydroxy ketone dehydrates readily because the new C=C is conjugated with both the ring and C=O, giving the E-enone.
keyPoints: Aromatic aldehyde acts only as electrophile (no α-H)
Dehydration is spontaneous because of extended conjugation
Product is mainly trans (E)
Excess benzaldehyde with acetone gives dibenzalacetone
whenUsed: Making chalcones, cinnamaldehyde and related conjugated enones.
jeeTips: Do not confuse with Cannizzaro: that needs conc. NaOH and no other carbonyl with α-H. Use dilute NaOH and a ketone with α-H for Claisen–Schmidt. Product is always the dehydrated enone.

name: Cannizzaro Reaction
summary: Aldehydes with no α-hydrogen undergo disproportionation in concentrated alkali: one molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate and the other reduced to the alcohol.
mechanism: Hydroxide adds to C=O of one molecule to give a tetrahedral anion. This transfers a hydride (H-) to the carbonyl carbon of a second aldehyde molecule, forming carboxylic acid (as carboxylate) and alkoxide, which is protonated to the alcohol.
keyPoints: Substrate must lack α-H (HCHO, ArCHO, (CH3)3CCHO)
Self-Cannizzaro gives 1:1 alcohol and acid salt
Rate is second order in aldehyde and first order in OH-
Hydride transfer is the key step (shown by D incorporation studies: no solvent D in the alcohol C–H)
whenUsed: Preparation of benzyl alcohol and benzoic acid; disproportionation of HCHO.
jeeTips: Acetaldehyde (has α-H) gives aldol, not Cannizzaro. Maximum yield of alcohol is 50% in self-Cannizzaro. The alcohol H comes from the other aldehyde, not solvent. Reduced product is alcohol, oxidised product is acid salt (acidify to get acid).

name: Crossed Cannizzaro Reaction
summary: Cannizzaro reaction between two different non-enolisable aldehydes; formaldehyde is oxidised preferentially (sacrificial reductant), so the other aldehyde is fully reduced to the alcohol.
mechanism: Hydroxide adds to the more electrophilic HCHO to give a hydrate anion which acts as the hydride donor. The hydride is transferred to the less reactive but suitable acceptor ArCHO, giving ArCH2OH and formate.
keyPoints: Formaldehyde is the best hydride donor (most easily hydrated)
Other aldehyde ends up as alcohol in about 100% yield
Both aldehydes must be non-enolisable
Final step of pentaerythritol synthesis
whenUsed: High-yield reduction of ArCHO to ArCH2OH; synthesis of pentaerythritol.
jeeTips: In a crossed Cannizzaro with HCHO, the product from HCHO is always formate and the other aldehyde gives alcohol. Do not say both give alcohol and acid.

name: Tishchenko Reaction
summary: Two molecules of an aldehyde disproportionate to an ester under aluminium alkoxide catalysis, a non-aqueous alternative to the Cannizzaro reaction.
mechanism: The aldehyde coordinates to Al of the alkoxide and the alkoxide adds to C=O to give a hemiacetal alkoxide. Intramolecular hydride transfer from this to a second coordinated aldehyde gives the ester and regenerates the catalyst.
keyPoints: Works for aldehydes with or without α-H
Product is an ester of the corresponding acid and alcohol
Uses aluminium alkoxide, not aqueous base
Industrial route to ethyl acetate from acetaldehyde
whenUsed: Industrial ethyl acetate and benzyl benzoate synthesis.
jeeTips: Link: Cannizzaro (aq. NaOH) gives alcohol + acid salt; Tishchenko (Al(OR)3) gives ester. Acetaldehyde, which fails Cannizzaro, works here.

name: Perkin Reaction
summary: Condensation of an aromatic aldehyde with an acid anhydride having α-H in presence of the sodium salt of the same acid gives an α,β-unsaturated aromatic acid.
mechanism: Acetate removes an α-H of acetic anhydride to give an enolate, which attacks ArCHO (aldol type). Acylation, then elimination of acetate, gives the unsaturated mixed anhydride, which hydrolyses to cinnamic acid.
keyPoints: Aromatic aldehyde has no α-H
Anhydride must have at least two α-H (R-CH2-CO)2O to allow dehydration
The salt used should match the anhydride's acid
Product: trans-cinnamic acid; α-substituent comes from anhydride (propionic anhydride gives α-methylcinnamic acid)
whenUsed: Synthesis of cinnamic acids and coumarin (from salicylaldehyde).
jeeTips: Distinguish from Claisen–Schmidt: Perkin uses anhydride + its sodium salt and gives an acid. Ketone partner is not used. Electron-withdrawing groups on the ring speed up the reaction.

name: Knoevenagel Condensation
summary: Condensation of an aldehyde or ketone with an active methylene compound (Z-CH2-Z') using a weak amine base gives an α,β-unsaturated compound after loss of water.
mechanism: The weak base removes a highly acidic CH2 proton (flanked by two EWG) to give a stabilised carbanion. It adds to the carbonyl, and the β-hydroxy adduct dehydrates (E1cB). In the Doebner variant with malonic acid in pyridine, decarboxylation follows to give cinnamic acids.
keyPoints: Active methylene: malonic ester, acetoacetic ester, malononitrile, CH2(CN)COOEt
Weak base avoids self-aldol of aldehyde
Doebner: ArCHO + CH2(COOH)2 / pyridine gives ArCH=CHCOOH + CO2
Product is conjugated and usually E
whenUsed: Mild synthesis of cinnamic acids and unsaturated nitriles/esters.
jeeTips: Key word: active methylene plus weak base (piperidine/pyridine). Strong base would cause Cannizzaro/aldol. Doebner modification loses CO2.

name: Benzoin Condensation
summary: Two molecules of an aromatic aldehyde couple in presence of cyanide catalyst to give an α-hydroxy ketone (acyloin), benzoin.
mechanism: Cyanide adds to PhCHO to give a cyanohydrin anion. Proton transfer gives a carbanion (acyl anion equivalent, umpolung) which attacks a second PhCHO. Loss of CN- from the adduct regenerates catalyst and gives benzoin.
keyPoints: Cyanide is a catalyst and reverses polarity (umpolung)
Aromatic aldehydes only (aliphatic ones give cyanohydrins/aldol)
Benzoin can be oxidised by HNO3 or Fehling to benzil
Benzil with conc. KOH gives benzilic acid
whenUsed: Making α-hydroxy ketones and then benzil / benzilic acid.
applications: Benzoin to benzil to benzilic acid sequence
jeeTips: Benzoin is a ketone with α-OH and reduces Fehling/Tollens (acyloin). Do not confuse with benzoic acid or benzil. Reaction needs a ring-bound CHO; HCHO/CH3CHO do not do this.

name: Rosenmund Reduction
catalyst: Pd/BaSO4, partially poisoned by quinoline / S
summary: Selective catalytic hydrogenation of an acyl chloride to an aldehyde over palladium on barium sulfate poisoned with quinoline or sulphur.
mechanism: Hydrogenolysis of the C–Cl bond on the Pd surface replaces Cl with H. Barium sulphate (low surface area) and the poison reduce the catalyst activity so the aldehyde is not further reduced to alcohol.
keyPoints: Starts from an acid chloride, not acid or ester
Poison prevents over-reduction to RCH2OH
HCl is by-product
Cannot make HCHO (HCOCl unstable)
whenUsed: Conversion of acid chlorides to aldehydes, including aromatic aldehydes.
jeeTips: Without poison, you get primary alcohol (or hydrocarbon). Compare with Stephen (nitrile, SnCl2/HCl) and DIBAL-H (ester/nitrile). Rosenmund cannot give formaldehyde.

name: Stephen Reduction
conditions: Dry ether, HCl gas; then hydrolysis
summary: Nitriles are reduced by stannous chloride and HCl to an aldimine hydrochloride (tin chloride complex), which is hydrolysed by water to the aldehyde.
mechanism: HCl protonates the nitrile; SnCl2 transfers electrons/hydrogen to give an imine salt RCH=NH.HCl (as stannichloride). Hydrolysis of the iminium releases RCHO and NH4Cl.
keyPoints: Chain length unchanged from nitrile
Aromatic nitriles work best
Must be hydrolysed in a second step
Stops at aldehyde stage; LiAlH4 would give amine
whenUsed: Conversion of RCN to RCHO.
jeeTips: Written as RCN -> RCHO with SnCl2/HCl then H3O+. Aldehyde carbon comes from the CN carbon. Do not confuse with Etard or Gattermann.

name: Etard Reaction
conditions: CS2 or CCl4 solvent; hydrolysis of chromium complex
summary: Toluene is oxidised to benzaldehyde by chromyl chloride in CS2 or CCl4; the intermediate brown Etard complex is hydrolysed to the aldehyde.
mechanism: CrO2Cl2 inserts into/ abstracts H from the benzylic C–H giving a chromium complex [ArCH(OCrOHCl2)2]. Hydrolysis of this complex (not oxidation further) gives ArCHO, avoiding over-oxidation to acid.
keyPoints: Reagent: CrO2Cl2 (chromyl chloride)
Complex isolable (brown) and hydrolysed with H2O
Prevents over-oxidation to benzoic acid
Works on side-chain methyl of toluene and homologues
whenUsed: Selective oxidation of an aryl methyl group to CHO.
jeeTips: Reagent is chromyl chloride, not chromyl chloride test reagent K2Cr2O7. Compare CrO3/Ac2O (gives benzylidene diacetate), KMnO4 (gives acid), and Cl2/hv then hydrolysis.

name: Gattermann–Koch Reaction
summary: Formylation of benzene and alkylbenzenes with CO and HCl in presence of anhydrous AlCl3 and cuprous chloride gives aromatic aldehydes.
mechanism: CO and HCl form formyl chloride (HCOCl), unstable on its own, which with AlCl3 gives the formyl cation HCO+ (electrophile). Electrophilic aromatic substitution at the ring gives ArCHO.
keyPoints: Electrophile: HCO+
Works for benzene, toluene, xylene (para product from toluene)
Fails for phenols and phenol ethers, and deactivated rings
CuCl acts as carrier of CO at ordinary pressure
whenUsed: Direct ring formylation of benzene, toluene.
jeeTips: Compare with Gattermann (HCN/HCl) which also works for phenols. Gattermann–Koch gives para isomer with alkylbenzenes. Substrates with strongly activating OH/OR usually not used here.

name: Gattermann Aldehyde Synthesis
conditions: Zn(CN)2 may replace HCN, then H3O+
summary: Aromatic compounds are formylated by HCN and HCl with Lewis acid; the intermediate aldimine hydrochloride is hydrolysed to the aldehyde.
mechanism: HCN + HCl gives formimidoyl chloride HN=CHCl, which with AlCl3 gives the electrophile HC+=NH. Electrophilic substitution gives ArCH=NH.HCl, hydrolysed by water to ArCHO.
keyPoints: Extension of Gattermann–Koch (HCN replaces CO)
Phenols, phenolic ethers and more reactive rings can be formylated
Zn(CN)2 / HCl is the safer in-situ HCN
Intermediate is an aldimine, hydrolysed to CHO
whenUsed: Formylation of phenols, ethers and heteroarenes.
jeeTips: Remember: Gattermann–Koch = CO/HCl; Gattermann = HCN/HCl (or Zn(CN)2). Gattermann is not Gattermann reaction of diazonium salts (Cu powder, HX), which gives aryl halides.

name: Oxidation of Toluene with CrO3 / Acetic Anhydride
summary: Toluene is oxidised by CrO3 in acetic anhydride to benzylidene diacetate (a gem-diacetate), a stable protected aldehyde that on acid hydrolysis gives benzaldehyde.
mechanism: CrO3 and Ac2O form chromyl acetate, which oxidises the benzylic CH3 to CH(OAc)2. The acetic anhydride esterifies the intermediate gem-diol, protecting it from further oxidation to benzoic acid. Hydrolysis with dilute acid releases ArCHO.
keyPoints: Product is protected aldehyde (acylal)
Ac2O prevents over-oxidation to benzoic acid
Needs hydrolysis (H3O+) for benzaldehyde
Alternative to Étard and Cl2/hv-hydrolysis routes
whenUsed: Laboratory and industrial preparation of benzaldehyde from toluene.
jeeTips: Remember the intermediate: benzylidene diacetate, not benzoic acid. Compare Etard (CrO2Cl2/CS2) and KMnO4 (gives benzoic acid).

name: Wolff–Kishner Reduction
summary: Carbonyl is converted to a CH2 group by heating with hydrazine and KOH in a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol; it is the basic-medium method of deoxygenation.
mechanism: Hydrazine condenses with C=O to give a hydrazone. Base removes N–H protons; the resulting anion tautomerises and loses N2 irreversibly to give a carbanion which is protonated by solvent to give the alkane.
keyPoints: Basic conditions: use for acid-sensitive substrates
Hydrazone is the intermediate
Driving force is evolution of N2
Alternative of Clemmensen (acidic)
whenUsed: Deoxygenation of aldehydes/ketones, especially acid-sensitive ones.
jeeTips: Choose Wolff–Kishner (NH2NH2/KOH) for substrates containing acid-labile groups (acetals, alkenes that add HCl) and Clemmensen (Zn-Hg/HCl) for base-labile ones. Haloalkyl or ester groups may react in base.

name: Clemmensen Reduction
summary: Reduction of aldehydes and ketones to the corresponding hydrocarbons using zinc amalgam and concentrated hydrochloric acid.
mechanism: Reduction occurs on the zinc surface, probably via zinc carbenoid species, with electron transfer and protonation. The C=O oxygen is removed as water; the alcohol is not an intermediate.
keyPoints: Acidic conditions: avoid acid-sensitive groups
Works best for aryl alkyl ketones (e.g. from Friedel–Crafts acylation)
Alcohol is not an intermediate
Complementary to Wolff–Kishner
whenUsed: Reduction of Friedel–Crafts acylation products to straight-chain alkylbenzenes.
jeeTips: Friedel–Crafts alkylation with n-propyl chloride gives isopropylbenzene due to rearrangement, so acylation then Clemmensen is used to get n-propylbenzene. Reagent is Zn-Hg, not Zn dust.

name: Meerwein–Ponndorf–Verley (MPV) Reduction
summary: Selective reduction of aldehydes and ketones to alcohols using aluminium isopropoxide in isopropanol; it is the reverse of Oppenauer oxidation.
mechanism: The carbonyl O coordinates to Al; a hydride is transferred from the isopropoxide C–H to the carbonyl carbon through a six-membered cyclic transition state. Acetone is released and distilled out to drive equilibrium.
keyPoints: C=C and other reducible groups are untouched
Reversible; acetone removal shifts to products
Six-membered chair TS, hydride transfer
Reverse of Oppenauer oxidation
whenUsed: Chemoselective carbonyl reduction in the presence of C=C, NO2 or halogens.
applications: Reduction of crotonaldehyde to crotyl alcohol
jeeTips: Key trap: C=C and NO2 are not reduced (unlike H2/Ni or LiAlH4/NaBH4 for NO2/alkene cases). Hydride comes from the alcohol C–H. Opposite reaction: Oppenauer.

name: Oppenauer Oxidation
summary: Mild, selective oxidation of secondary alcohols to ketones using aluminium alkoxide and an excess of acetone (hydride acceptor); reverse of MPV reduction.
mechanism: Alcohol exchanges with the Al alkoxide; acetone coordinates to Al; hydride is transferred from the alkoxide C–H to acetone through a six-membered TS. Large excess of acetone pushes the equilibrium toward the ketone.
keyPoints: Reverse of MPV reduction
Does not oxidise C=C (selective)
Best for secondary alcohols; primary alcohols give aldehydes that suffer aldol
Excess acetone is the oxidant
whenUsed: Oxidation of allylic/steroid secondary alcohols without touching C=C.
jeeTips: Pair MPV and Oppenauer as reverse reactions of the same aluminium alkoxide. Acetone is the oxidant, not a solvent only. Does not oxidise C=C or form acids.

name: Haloform (Iodoform) Reaction
summary: Methyl ketones (and acetaldehyde, ethanol, and CH3CH(OH)R) react with I2/NaOH or NaOX to give a haloform and the sodium carboxylate with one carbon less.
mechanism: Base-promoted enolisation and α-halogenation occur three times on the CH3 group (each halogenation makes the next H more acidic) to give R-CO-CI3. Hydroxide attacks C=O, expelling CI3- (good leaving group due to three I), which is protonated to CHI3 to give RCOO-.
keyPoints: Needs CH3-CO- or CH3-CH(OH)- group
Product acid has one carbon less than starting methyl ketone
CHI3 is yellow solid, m.p. 392 K, antiseptic smell
Positive: acetaldehyde, ethanol, acetone, acetophenone, 2-butanol; Negative: methanol, HCHO, 3-pentanone
whenUsed: Test for CH3CO / CH3CH(OH) groups, and conversion of methyl ketones to acids.
applications: Conversion of RCOCH3 to RCOOH (one carbon less)

examples.eq: CH3COCH3 + 3 I2 + 4 NaOH -> CHI3 + CH3COONa + 3 NaI + 3 H2O

examples.note: Benzoic acid from acetophenone using NaOCl

examples.eq: CH3CH2OH + 4 I2 + 6 NaOH -> CHI3 + HCOONa + 5 NaI + 5 H2O

jeeTips: Ethanol is the only primary alcohol that gives it; acetaldehyde is the only aldehyde. Acetophenone gives benzoate. 3-Pentanone, CH3CH2COCH2CH3, is negative. CH3COOH and esters (ethyl acetate) fail. Yellow ppt of CHI3 (m.p. 119 °C).

name: Tollens' Test
summary: Aldehydes (aliphatic and aromatic) reduce ammoniacal silver nitrate to metallic silver (silver mirror); ketones do not respond.
mechanism: The aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate by Ag+ (as diamminesilver(I)); Ag+ is reduced to Ag(0), which deposits as a bright mirror on clean glass.
keyPoints: Positive for all aldehydes (also formic acid, glucose, α-hydroxy ketones such as benzoin/fructose)
Ketones negative (except α-hydroxy ketones)
Alkaline medium; test tube must be very clean
Differentiates aldehyde from ketone
whenUsed: Distinguishing aldehydes from ketones.

examples.eq: CH3CHO + 2 [Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3 OH- -> CH3COO- + 2 Ag + 4 NH3 + 2 H2O
C6H5CHO + 2 [Ag(NH3)2]+ + 3 OH- -> C6H5COO- + 2 Ag + 4 NH3 + 2 H2O
HCOOH + 2 [Ag(NH3)2]+ + 2 OH- -> CO2 + 2 Ag + 4 NH3 + 2 H2O

jeeTips: Both aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes give silver mirror (unlike Fehling's). Ketones negative but α-hydroxy ketones (acyloins, fructose) are positive. Oxidant: Ag+ is reduced, not NH3.

name: Fehling's Test
reagents: Fehling's solution (Cu2+ in alkaline sodium potassium tartrate)
catalyst: Fehling's A (CuSO4) + Fehling's B (Rochelle salt + NaOH)
summary: Aliphatic aldehydes reduce the blue Cu(II)-tartrate complex to red-brown cuprous oxide; aromatic aldehydes and ketones do not respond.
mechanism: Tartrate keeps Cu2+ in solution in alkaline medium. Aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate while Cu(II) is reduced to Cu(I) as Cu2O.
keyPoints: Positive: aliphatic aldehydes, reducing sugars, formic acid
Negative: aromatic aldehydes (benzaldehyde), ketones
Solution freshly mixed from A and B
Colour changes blue to red-brown precipitate
whenUsed: Distinguishing aliphatic from aromatic aldehydes.

examples.eq: CH3CHO + 2 Cu2+ + 5 OH- -> CH3COO- + Cu2O + 3 H2O
HCHO + 2 Cu2+ + 5 OH- -> HCOO- + Cu2O + 3 H2O

jeeTips: Benzaldehyde does NOT respond to Fehling's but does to Tollens'. Ketones are negative for both except α-hydroxy ketones (glucose/fructose positive). Alkaline medium needed.

name: Benedict's Test
summary: Benedict's solution (milder alkaline Cu(II) citrate) is reduced by aliphatic aldehydes and reducing sugars to red Cu2O; aromatic aldehydes and ketones do not respond.
mechanism: Citrate keeps Cu2+ in solution in mildly alkaline sodium carbonate. Aldehyde reduces Cu(II) to Cu(I) as Cu2O on heating, itself being oxidised to the acid salt.
keyPoints: Single reagent solution (more stable than Fehling's)
Used for reducing sugars (glucose positive)
Aromatic aldehydes negative
Citrate replaces tartrate; Na2CO3 replaces NaOH
whenUsed: Detecting reducing sugars and aliphatic aldehydes.

examples.eq: CH3CHO + 2 Cu2+ + 5 OH- -> CH3COO- + Cu2O + 3 H2O

jeeTips: Benedict's and Fehling's behave alike; difference is the complexing agent (citrate versus tartrate) and the milder alkali (Na2CO3). Sucrose is non-reducing and gives no ppt.

name: Schiff's Test
summary: Aldehydes restore the pink colour of Schiff's reagent (rosaniline hydrochloride decolourised by SO2) in the cold; most ketones do not respond.
mechanism: The aldehyde reacts with the leuco sulphonic acid form of the dye (aminosulphinic acid), forming a coloured addition product that restores the magenta quinoid chromophore.
keyPoints: Positive for aldehydes (aliphatic and aromatic)
Acetone and other ketones are negative
Test must be done in the cold and neutral/acidic medium
Formaldehyde colour persists in conc. H2SO4 while others fade
whenUsed: Detecting an aldehyde group.
applications: HCHO colour retained on adding H2SO4

examples.eq: RCHO + Schiff's reagent -> pink / magenta colour
HCHO ->[Schiff's reagent] Magenta persists with conc. H2SO4

jeeTips: Acetone gives a faint pink colour only after long standing; use fresh reagent. Do not heat or add alkali: decomposition of reagent gives false positive.

name: 2,4-DNP (Brady's) Test
summary: Aldehydes and ketones give a yellow, orange or red precipitate of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone; the test is for the C=O group generally.
mechanism: The NH2 of 2,4-DNPH adds to C=O (nucleophilic addition) to give a carbinolamine, which eliminates water to form the C=N bond of the hydrazone (addition–elimination), catalysed by acid.
keyPoints: Positive for all aldehydes and ketones
Carboxylic acids, esters and amides are negative (resonance reduces C=O electrophilicity)
Melting point of the derivative identifies the carbonyl compound
Not a test to separate aldehydes and ketones
whenUsed: Detecting C=O in aldehydes/ketones and characterising by derivative melting point.
jeeTips: Positive for both aldehydes AND ketones; combine with Tollens to separate them. Carboxylic acid derivatives (C=O of COOH, ester, amide) do not respond. Colour: yellow (unconjugated) to red (conjugated aromatic).

name: Wittig Reaction
conditions: Ylide made from Ph3P + RX then BuLi/NaH
summary: Aldehydes and ketones are converted into alkenes by phosphorus ylides (Wittig reagents), with the C=O oxygen replaced by =CR2.
mechanism: Ph3P attacks an alkyl halide (SN2) to give a phosphonium salt; a strong base removes an α-H to give the ylide. The ylide carbon attacks C=O to form a betaine/oxaphosphetane, which collapses to alkene and Ph3P=O (strong P=O bond is the driving force).
keyPoints: Position of the new C=C is fixed (no mixture of isomers)
Non-stabilised ylides give mostly Z alkenes; stabilised ylides give E
Ylide from Ph3P + CH3I + BuLi gives methylenation
By-product Ph3P=O drives the reaction
whenUsed: Regiospecific alkene synthesis from carbonyls.
applications: Synthesis of stilbene, vitamin A intermediates

examples.eq: Ph3P+CH3 Br- + BuLi -> Ph3P=CH2 + LiBr + BuH

jeeTips: Wittig fixes the double bond position, unlike dehydration of alcohols (Saytzeff mixtures). Ylide: Ph3P=CH2 gives terminal alkene. The O goes to P as Ph3P=O.

name: Baeyer–Villiger Oxidation
summary: Ketones are converted into esters (cyclic ketones into lactones) by peracids through insertion of an oxygen atom next to the carbonyl carbon.
mechanism: Peracid adds to C=O to give the Criegee intermediate. Concerted migration of a group with its bonding pair from carbon to the adjacent electron-deficient oxygen, with loss of carboxylic acid, gives the ester. Migration retains configuration of the migrating carbon.
keyPoints: Migratory aptitude: tertiary > cyclohexyl > secondary > benzyl ~ phenyl > primary > methyl > H
Group that migrates ends attached to oxygen
Retention of configuration at migrating centre
Aldehydes (H migrates) give carboxylic acids
whenUsed: Converting ketones to esters / lactones, e.g. cyclohexanone to ε-caprolactone, ketone to alcohol (after hydrolysis).
jeeTips: Migratory aptitude decides product: acetophenone gives phenyl acetate (CH3COOPh), not methyl benzoate. With a methyl ketone and a tertiary alkyl, t-alkyl migrates. Benzaldehyde gives benzoic acid (aryl or H migrates).

name: Beckmann Rearrangement
summary: Ketoximes rearrange in acid to N-substituted amides (cyclic ketoximes give lactams).
mechanism: The oxime OH is converted into a good leaving group (protonation or phosphorylation). The group anti to the leaving group migrates from C to N as water leaves (concerted). The resulting nitrilium ion adds water and tautomerises to the amide.
keyPoints: Anti-group to OH migrates (stereospecific)
Cyclohexanone oxime gives caprolactam (nylon-6 monomer)
Aldoximes give nitriles or amides
Acetophenone oxime (E) gives acetanilide
whenUsed: Industrial caprolactam for nylon-6.
jeeTips: Know which group is anti: for E-acetophenone oxime (OH anti to phenyl), phenyl migrates to give acetanilide (CH3CONHPh), not N-methylbenzamide. Do not confuse with Hofmann bromamide rearrangement.

name: Cyanohydrin Formation (HCN Addition)
summary: Aldehydes and most ketones add HCN to give cyanohydrins (α-hydroxynitriles) - a nucleophilic addition that adds one carbon.
mechanism: Base generates CN-, which attacks C=O to give an alkoxide; the alkoxide is protonated by HCN regenerating CN-. The reaction is reversible; electron-poor, unhindered carbonyls give best yields.
keyPoints: Catalysed by base (CN- is the actual nucleophile)
Reactivity: HCHO > RCHO > R2CO; hindered ketones poor
Adds one carbon; nitrile hydrolyses to α-hydroxy acid
Creates a chiral centre (racemic mixture with prochiral carbonyl)
whenUsed: Chain extension, preparation of α-hydroxy acids (lactic acid).
jeeTips: Pure HCN is poorly nucleophilic; catalytic NaOH/NaCN is needed. Excess acid reduces CN- and retards reaction. Product from aldehyde is racemic (d,l).

name: Sodium Bisulphite Addition
productName: Bisulphite addition compound (α-hydroxy sulphonate, white crystals)
summary: Aldehydes, methyl ketones and small cyclic ketones add NaHSO3 to give crystalline α-hydroxy sulphonate salts, used to separate and purify carbonyls.
mechanism: The nucleophilic sulphur of HSO3- attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide that is protonated to give the sulphonate. Adduct is regenerated to the carbonyl by dil. acid or alkali.
keyPoints: Works with aldehydes, methyl ketones (CH3COR), cyclic ketones up to 8-membered
Bulky ketones (diaryl, tert-alkyl) do not react
Reversible: dilute acid or Na2CO3 regenerates carbonyl
Used for separation/purification
whenUsed: Purification of aldehydes/methyl ketones from mixtures.

examples.eq: CH3CH(OH)SO3Na + HCl -> CH3CHO + NaCl + SO2 + H2O

jeeTips: Benzophenone and acetophenone (bulky) do not form bisulphite adducts, nor does 3-pentanone. Sulphur (not oxygen) bonds to carbon.

name: Formation of Oximes, Hydrazones and Semicarbazones (Ammonia Derivatives)
conditions: Z = OH, NH2, NHPh, NHCONH2, NH-C6H3(NO2)2
summary: Carbonyls react with NH2OH, NH2NH2, PhNHNH2 and NH2CONHNH2 to give C=N derivatives (oximes, hydrazones, semicarbazones) by addition–elimination with loss of water.
mechanism: Amine nitrogen adds to C=O to form a carbinolamine, which is protonated on O and loses water to form C=N. Mild acid catalysis (pH about 4–5) is optimal: stronger acid protonates the nucleophile, weaker acid does not activate C=O.
keyPoints: Optimum pH about 4.5
Products are crystalline derivatives with sharp melting points (identification)
Semicarbazone: NH2NHCONH2 attacks through NH2 attached to the NH not the amide
Z = OH gives oxime; NH2 hydrazone; NHPh phenylhydrazone; NHCONH2 semicarbazone
whenUsed: Characterisation of carbonyl compounds; Beckmann and Wolff–Kishner precursors.
jeeTips: The reaction needs mildly acidic medium, not strongly acidic or strongly basic. Only the terminal NH2 of semicarbazide is nucleophilic (the other N is amide-like). Reactivity: HCHO > RCHO > R2CO.

name: Acetal / Ketal Formation (Protection with Ethylene Glycol)
summary: Aldehydes and ketones react with alcohols (or diols such as ethylene glycol) under dry acid catalysis to form acetals/ketals, which protect C=O from bases, nucleophiles, and hydrides.
mechanism: The carbonyl O is protonated; alcohol adds to give a hemiacetal; protonation and loss of water gives an oxocarbenium ion, which is attacked by a second OH to give the acetal. Removal of water drives equilibrium; dilute aqueous acid hydrolyses the acetal back.
keyPoints: Stable to bases, Grignards, LiAlH4, NaBH4
Hydrolysed by dilute aqueous acid back to carbonyl
Ethylene glycol gives a cyclic five-membered 1,3-dioxolane
Dry HCl needed (aqueous acid reverses reaction)
whenUsed: Protecting group chemistry in multistep synthesis.
applications: Selective reduction of an ester in presence of a ketone

examples.eq: CH3COCH2CH2COOC2H5 ->[1. HOCH2CH2OH, H+][2. LiAlH4][3. H3O+] CH3COCH2CH2CH2OH

jeeTips: Acetals are ethers of gem-diol: stable in base, labile in acid. Remember protect C=O, reduce ester, then deprotect. Hemiacetal is unstable and not isolated (except in sugars).

name: Reformatsky Reaction
summary: An α-halo ester with zinc forms an organozinc enolate which adds to an aldehyde or ketone to give a β-hydroxy ester (and dehydration gives α,β-unsaturated ester).
mechanism: Zn inserts into the C–Br bond of the α-bromo ester to give a zinc enolate (Reformatsky reagent), less reactive than Grignards so it does not attack the ester group. It adds to the carbonyl; acid work-up gives the β-hydroxy ester.
keyPoints: Organozinc is less reactive than RMgX: ester not attacked
Products: β-hydroxy esters (heated: α,β-unsaturated esters)
Aldehydes and ketones both work
Alternative to aldol with ester enolates
whenUsed: Synthesis of β-hydroxy esters.
jeeTips: Zn is used because Mg would attack the ester group. The product is β-hydroxy (not α-hydroxy) ester.

name: Michael Addition
summary: A stabilised carbanion (Michael donor) adds in a 1,4-fashion to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl or nitrile (Michael acceptor) to give a 1,5-dicarbonyl compound.
mechanism: Base forms an enolate from the active methylene donor. The enolate attacks the β-carbon of the enone (conjugate addition) to give a new enolate, which is protonated to give the saturated adduct.
keyPoints: Donor: active methylene (malonate, acetoacetate, β-diketones)
Acceptor: enone, enoate, acrylonitrile, nitroalkene
1,4-Addition, giving 1,5-dicarbonyl
Followed by intramolecular aldol is Robinson annulation
whenUsed: C–C bond formation at the β-position; Robinson annulation.
jeeTips: Michael = 1,4 (conjugate) addition. Grignard/RLi give 1,2-addition while Gilman reagents R2CuLi and soft nucleophiles give 1,4. A 1,5-dicarbonyl product signals a Michael step.

name: Mannich Reaction
summary: Three-component condensation of an enolisable carbonyl compound, formaldehyde and a primary or secondary amine to give a β-amino carbonyl (Mannich base).
mechanism: The amine and HCHO condense to form an iminium ion (CH2=N+R2). The enol of the ketone attacks the iminium carbon, giving the β-amino ketone after loss of H+.
keyPoints: Three components: C–H acid, non-enolisable aldehyde (HCHO), amine
Product is a β-amino ketone
Iminium ion is the electrophile
Mannich base on heating gives α,β-unsaturated ketone by loss of amine
whenUsed: Synthesis of β-amino carbonyls and alkaloids.
jeeTips: Primary or secondary amine (not tertiary) is used; formaldehyde is the aldehyde. Count the product: C–H acid + CH2 + amine, minus water.

name: Benzilic Acid Rearrangement
summary: 1,2-Diketones (benzil) rearrange in strong base to α-hydroxy carboxylic acids (benzilic acid) by 1,2-aryl shift.
mechanism: Hydroxide adds to one C=O to give a tetrahedral alkoxide. A phenyl group migrates with its electron pair to the neighbouring carbonyl carbon (1,2-shift), forming a carboxylate and an alkoxide. Acidification gives benzilic acid.
keyPoints: Starts from a 1,2-diketone
Net: 1,2-aryl (alkyl) shift
Hydroxide is a reagent (not just a catalyst), consumed as carboxylate
Product is an α-hydroxy acid (tertiary alcohol)
whenUsed: Synthesis of α-hydroxy acids; part of benzoin to benzil to benzilic acid sequence.
applications: Benzoin to benzil to benzilic acid
jeeTips: Cyclic 1,2-diketones undergo ring contraction. Do not confuse with pinacol (diol to ketone) or Cannizzaro (intermolecular hydride shift).

name: Riley Oxidation (SeO2)
summary: Selenium dioxide oxidises the α-CH2 or CH3 of a carbonyl compound to give a 1,2-dicarbonyl (and allylic CH to allylic alcohol/enone).
mechanism: The enol form attacks SeO2 at Se (ene-type); loss of water and a [2,3]-sigmatropic shift or hydrolysis leads to the α-keto compound. Se(IV) is reduced to red/black elemental selenium.
keyPoints: SeO2 oxidises CH2/CH3 adjacent to C=O to C=O
Allylic CH2 oxidised to alcohol or carbonyl
Elemental Se is black or red by-product
Acetaldehyde to glyoxal; acetone to methylglyoxal; acetophenone to phenylglyoxal
whenUsed: Preparing 1,2-dicarbonyl compounds.
jeeTips: Note: SeO2 oxidises α-CH3/CH2 to C=O, not the carbonyl itself. A black/red deposit of Se is the visual cue. Toxic reagent.

name: DIBAL-H Reduction of Esters / Nitriles to Aldehydes
summary: DIBAL-H at low temperature (-78 °C) reduces esters and nitriles to aldehydes (after aqueous work-up) without over-reduction to alcohol/amine.
mechanism: The Lewis acidic Al coordinates the C=O oxygen (or the nitrile N) and delivers hydride once. At -78 °C the tetrahedral aluminium hemiacetal (or imine-aluminium) intermediate is stable and does not eliminate; aqueous work-up releases the aldehyde.
keyPoints: One equivalent at -78 °C is key
Warmer or excess DIBAL gives primary alcohol
Nitriles give aldehydes via imine hydrolysis
Bulky, electrophilic hydride (unlike LiAlH4 which over-reduces)
whenUsed: Controlled partial reduction of esters/nitriles to aldehydes.

examples.eq: CH3COOC2H5 ->[1. DIBAL-H, -78 C][2. H3O+] CH3CHO + C2H5OH

jeeTips: LiAlH4 would give alcohol/amine; DIBAL-H at low temperature stops at aldehyde. Compare Stephen (nitrile) and Rosenmund (acid chloride).

name: Wacker Process
summary: Industrial oxidation of ethene to acetaldehyde by oxygen in water with PdCl2 catalyst and CuCl2 as co-catalyst (re-oxidant).
mechanism: Pd(II) coordinates ethene; water attacks (hydroxypalladation) and β-hydride elimination gives acetaldehyde and Pd(0). Pd(0) is re-oxidised to Pd(II) by Cu(II), and Cu(I) is re-oxidised by O2.
keyPoints: Catalyst cycle: Pd(II) to Pd(0), Cu(II) to Cu(I), O2 regenerates Cu(II)
Terminal alkenes give methyl ketones (propene to acetone)
Oxygen of C=O comes from water
Acetaldehyde is key intermediate to acetic acid
whenUsed: Large-scale acetaldehyde production.

examples.eq: CH2=CH2 + PdCl2 + H2O -> CH3CHO + Pd + 2 HCl

jeeTips: Overall: ethene + 1/2 O2 gives acetaldehyde. Propene gives acetone (not propanal). Remember PdCl2 + CuCl2.

name: Favorskii Rearrangement
summary: α-Halo ketones with an α'-H rearrange in base to carboxylic acid derivatives; cyclic α-halo ketones undergo ring contraction.
mechanism: Base removes the α'-H giving an enolate that displaces halide intramolecularly (cyclopropanone intermediate). The nucleophile (OH- or OR-) opens the cyclopropanone to the more stable carbanion, which is protonated to give the acid or ester.
keyPoints: Requires α-halo ketone with α'-H
Cyclopropanone is the intermediate
Ring contraction of cyclic α-halo ketones (6 to 5)
Nucleophile determines product: OH- gives acid, OR- ester, NR2 amide
whenUsed: Ring contractions to strained rings (cubane, cyclopentane carboxylates).
jeeTips: Not to be confused with Haloform. Ring contraction by one carbon is a hallmark. If no α'-H, quasi-Favorskii (semibenzilic) occurs.

name: Darzens Glycidic Ester Condensation
products: R2C(-O-)CH-COOC2H5 (epoxide ring; α,β-epoxy ester) + NaCl + C2H5OH
summary: Aldehydes/ketones condense with α-halo esters in presence of a base to give α,β-epoxy esters (glycidic esters), which can be hydrolysed and decarboxylated to give homologous aldehydes/ketones.
mechanism: Base removes the acidic α-H of the chloroester to give a carbanion that adds to C=O (aldol-type). The resulting alkoxide displaces the neighbouring chloride intramolecularly (SN2, 3-exo-tet) to form the epoxide.
keyPoints: Aldol followed by intramolecular SN2
Product: α,β-epoxy ester
Hydrolysis then decarboxylation gives aldehyde/ketone with one more carbon
Base should not be nucleophilic toward ester (use matching alkoxide)
whenUsed: Chain extension of ketones to aldehydes.

examples.eq: glycidic ester ->[1. NaOH][2. H3O+, \Delta] R2CH-CHO + CO2

jeeTips: Tip: product is epoxide not the aldol. Compare with Reformatsky (Zn gives β-hydroxy ester) and Wittig. Use the same alkoxide as the ester to avoid transesterification.

name: Aldehydes/Ketones from Nitriles via Grignard Reagents (RMgX + RCN)
summary: Grignard reagents add once to the C≡N bond to give an imine salt, which on aqueous acid hydrolysis gives a ketone Aldehydes are not obtained this way (aldehydes need DIBAL-H/Stephen on the nitrile, or Grignard with HC(OEt)3).
mechanism: R–MgX adds across the C≡N to give an iminyl magnesium halide R'C(=NMgX)R, stable and not attacked again. Hydrolysis (H3O+) gives the imine and then the ketone with loss of NH3.
keyPoints: Gives ketones from nitriles (aldehydes need a different reagent, e.g. HC(OEt)3 or DIBAL on nitrile)
No over-addition because iminyl anion is unreactive
Carbonyl carbon comes from CN carbon
Net: R'CN + RMgX to R'COR
whenUsed: Synthesis of unsymmetrical ketones.
jeeTips: Grignard + nitrile gives KETONE (not aldehyde). For aldehyde, use HCN-free route: Stephen reduction or DIBAL-H. Grignard + HCOOEt gives secondary alcohol; Grignard + HCHO gives primary alcohol.
